question.text: This grandnephew of Julius Caesar was the first emperor and founder of the Roman Empire, and outlasted the Second Triumvirate.
question.clue: This ruler reportedly shouted at Quintilius Varus to "give me back my legions" after his forces lost the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest.

swap.leadin: This man was the first Roman emperor.
swap.text: Name this adopted son of Julius Caesar and member of the Second Triumvirate.
swap.clue: During his reign, the Pantheon was constructed on the commission of Marcus Agrippa.

question.text: The loss at Cannae triggered a change in Roman strategy, leading to final victory in this war at the Battle of Zama.
question.clue: The deadliest battle in this war saw Paullus and Varro drawn into a double encirclement and lose 50 000 men.

swap.leadin: Name some buildings constructed by the Romans.
swap.text: This stadium, which predated the Republic of Rome, had a large track that was used for chariot racing, but today only a patch of grassland remains.
swap.clue: Tacitus claimed the Great Fire started near this location, where a series of dolphins were flipped to count the number of times that quadrigas successfully made it past two turning points called metae.

question.leadin: This person's namesake "destruction horizon" was described by Mortimer Wheeler.
question.text: Name this queen of the Iceni (ai-SEN-ai). After she was flogged and her daughters were raped, she led an army which sacked the city of Camulodunum (kam-yoo-load-YOO-num).
question.clue: This whip-scarred ruler avenged the rape of two daughters according to the Annals of Tacitus, whose Agricola barely discusses this consort of Prasutagus sacking Camulodunum ("cam-oo-LOH-doo-num") and Londinium.

swap.leadin: A letter to Tacitus that described an eruption of this volcano detailed the death of the admiral of the Misenum fleet.
swap.text: Name this mountain near the Bay of Naples, whose AD 79 eruption destroyed the nearby town of Herculaneum.
swap.clue: Artifacts excavated from towns next to this feature were confined to a Secret Museum due to their incredibly erotic content.

question.leadin: Fans of this sport destroyed the Baths of Zeuxippus during one revolt.
question.text: Name this sport whose greens and blues factions attempted to install Hypatius as emperor while chanting "Victory!" in the Nika Riots.
question.answerHtml: chariot racing [or chariot races; prompt on partial answer]
question.clue: The Blue and Green factions of fans of this sport united against Justinian during the Nika riots.

swap.leadin: This man's wife drove over her dead father's body with a chariot in a road now known as the "Street of Crime."
swap.text: Name this man who usurped Servius Tullius to become king of Rome. He himself was popularly overthrown after his son Sextus raped a woman named Lucretia.
swap.answerHtml: Tarquin the Proud (or Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; prompt on Lucius Tarquinius)
swap.clue: This last king of Rome was legendarily deposed and exiled after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Collatinus.

question.leadin: Identify these other kings of Rome.
question.text: This second king of Rome is credited with establishing the religious traditions of the city including the Vestal Virgins and the cults of Mars and Jupiter.
question.clue: This king, the second to rule Rome. This Sabine king built the Temple of Janus and made January the first month, in addition to setting the calendar at 365 days.

swap.text: Tarquinius Superbus fled to this king of Clusium, whose campaign to reinstall the king was foiled by the determination of Mucius Scaevola.
swap.clue: This figure was saved from death when a would-be assassin mistook his scribe for him, and that assassin thrust his right hand into a fire in an act of defiance against this figure.

question.leadin: The Creed of Ulfilas and Letter of Auxentius give us the clearest picture of this set of teachings.
question.text: Name this heresy briefly exonerated by the Council of Jerusalem which was named after a priest opposed by Athanasius.
question.clue: The emperor Constantius espoused this belief, leading to its further condemnation at the First Council of Constantinople.

swap.text: Ancient inhabitants of modern day Tuscany, among their famous representatives are Lars Porsenna who attempted to reinstall Tarquin the Proud. They were the dominant civilization in Italy until the rise of the Romans
swap.clue: These people were organized into the Dodecapoli, twelve cities that formed their namesake league.

question.leadin: Answer the following about religion in ancient Rome.
question.text: Not to be confused with Saturnalia, this festival took place in mid-February and featured the sacrifice of a goat and a dog, after which the priests would run through town and slap people with the skin of the goat.
question.clue: This event originated when King Amulius ordered two men to be thrown into the Tiber River as punishment.

swap.leadin: Decabalus was the last independent leader of this region.
swap.text: Name this region that was conquered by Trajan, which he depicted in his column. It had its capital at Sarmizegetusa.
swap.clue: Soldiers of this region used the sickle-like falx during a war in which a bridge near the Iron Gates was built by Apollodorus.

question.leadin: Suetonius records how a ruler of this region, Ptolemy, was executed by Caligula because his purple cloak drew the attention of the crowd when he entered a theatre.
question.text: Name this region that, after its annexation by Claudius, was divided into the provinces of Tingitana and Caesariensis. Another king of this region, Bocchus I, betrayed his son-in-law, Jugurtha, to Sulla.
question.answerHtml: Mauretania [accept Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis; prompt on North Africa, Maghreb, Algeria, Morocco, or the Atlas Mountains by asking “what was the Roman name of the region?”]
question.clue: It's not Egypt, but a man named Ptolemy was the last Roman client king of this region; its earlier client kings included the Numidian prince Juba II.

swap.text: Alexander the Great's general Eumenes is paired with this rebel leader, who fought one of the earliest guerrilla wars in alliance with the Lusitani. He was betrayed and murdered by his general Perperna.
swap.clue: Along with his lieutenant Hirtuleius, he overthrew the governor Quintus Metellus Pius, and then was joined by Marcus Perpenna, though Perpenna eventually had this man murdered at a banquet.

question.leadin: Answer the following questions about the ritual of evocatio, in which a Roman general would "call forth" an enemy deity, offering it a cult at Rome and thereby depriving its city of divine protection.
question.text: The first recorded instance of evocatio was the transferal of Juno Regina from this city to the Aventine Hill. The supposed ten-year siege of this city, which fell in 396 B.C., is likely an artificial reference to the Trojan War.
question.clue: This city, home to the Grotta Campana tomb perhaps constructed by that king Tolumnius, was built around a sanctuary at Portonaccio with a life-size terracotta statue of Apollo attributed to Vulca.

swap.text: Name this class of gladiator that usually fought against the Hoplomachus or the Thraex; the similar Secutor was usually instead paired against the Retiarius [reh-tee-AR-ee-us].

question.leadin: A scholar of ancient Rome employed her expertise in this non-history-related profession to determine that classicists had been mistranslating the word "acus" ("AY-cuss").
question.text: Name this profession of Janet Stephens, who analyzed texts such as an epigram by Martial in which an enslaved woman with this profession named Plecusa is killed. Members of this profession used tools like vittae ("VIT-tee") and calamistra.
question.answerHtml: hairdressers [or hairstylists; or ornatrix; or ornatrices; prompt on stylists or salon workers or beauticians or people who cut hair; reject “barbers” or “maids” or “domestic workers”] {Acus is a catch-all term for several different tools, but in this context refers to a sewing needle used for weaving hair. Vittae are hair ribbons. Calamistra are curling irons.}

swap.leadin: In 274 he used the duplicity of the Gallic emperor Tetricus to win the Battle of Chalons-en-Champagne.
swap.text: Name this emperor who helped end the Crisis of the Third Century by defeating the Alamanni.
swap.clue: Zenobia's armies were defeated at Antioch and Emesa by this Roman Emperor, who laid siege to Palmyra and placed Zenobia in his triumphal procession.
